transcript.text: I am the operations lead at a tour company. Each month I tell our local partners how many guides to reserve in each destination for the month after next. If I reserve too few, we hire freelancers at the last minute for about three times the price; if I reserve too many, we pay a small fee for each guide we do not use. My director asked me for a machine learning model that forecasts how many bookings we will receive per destination each month. The table I shared is our booking export up to late February 2026: one row per booking with the booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether it had free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. I will use the result myself every month to fix the reservation. [shares bookings.csv]

**What I understood**
You need a monthly forecast of bookings per destination, two months ahead, so you can tell local partners how many guides to reserve. The cost of under-forecasting is hiring freelancers at ~3× the price; over-forecasting costs a small fee per unused guide. You’ll use the forecast yourself each month. Your data is a booking-level export (1,500 rows to late Feb 2026) with booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time, price, free-cancellation flag, and cancellation flag.

**The real problem**
The decision is *how many guides to reserve per destination for the month after next*. What’s not known yet is how well any forecast can hit the “cost tolerance” implied by that 3× vs. small-fee asymmetry. A plain point forecast isn’t enough—you need to know its typical error and whether it systematically undershoots or overshoots.

**Approach**
Instead of jumping straight to a black-box model, I’d start by turning the booking log into a destination–month panel with engineered features (rolling bookings, lead-time percentiles, cancellation rates, channel shares). That panel becomes the single source of truth for a time-aware model, for the exploratory analysis that builds trust, and for any future dashboard. The model will be trained on a rolling-origin holdout that mimics your real forecasting cadence, and evaluated on the cost-weighted error that matches your 3× under-forecast penalty.

**Plan (five steps)**
1. **Prepare the panel** – Aggregate bookings to destination × travel-month, create rolling features, lead-time distributions, cancellation rates, channel shares. *Check:* panel has one row per destination-month, no leakage (features only use data available at forecast date). *Stop when* the recipe runs cleanly on the latest month.
2. **Exploratory analysis** – Plot monthly volume by destination, lead-time curves, cancellation rates, channel mix. *Check:* patterns match your operational knowledge (peak seasons, typical lead times). *Stop when* you can explain every major swing.
3. **Model training with cost-aware metric** – Train a gradient-boosted model (or similar) on a rolling-origin split; optimise a weighted MAE where under-forecast errors count 3×. *Check:* back-test shows median absolute percentage error within your tolerance and no systematic bias. *Stop when* the holdout cost-weighted error plateaus.
4. **Monthly forecast delivery** – Package the model + recipe so you can re-run each month and get a fresh destination–month forecast two months out. *Stop when* the first live forecast matches the back-test quality.
5. **Monitor & recalibrate** – Track actuals vs. forecast each month; if cost-weighted error drifts, retrain with the expanded history. *Check:* quarterly review shows error stable or improving. *Stop when* the process is routine.

(That is the short version. Ask me about any part and I will go deeper.)

(I left out the parts whose numbers I cannot source from you or your data. Ask me about any part in words and I will go through it.)

choices.what: Build a model that predicts how many bookings will arrive for each destination in each future month, using the booking history up to the forecast date. The model learns from destination, seasonality, lead-time patterns, channel mix, and cancellation behaviour. You get: A monthly forecast per destination you can hand to partners two months ahead, plus a back-test showing how often the forecast would have been within your cost tolerance. Trade-off: Needs careful feature engineering (rolling windows, lead-time distributions) and a holdout that respects time; more effort upfront but gives you a number you can act on directly. Effort: Medium.

choices.title: Exploratory analysis of booking patterns
choices.what: Quantify the seasonality, lead-time distribution, cancellation rate, and channel mix for each destination, so you see exactly what drives volume and where the forecast uncertainty lives. You get: A set of charts and tables (monthly volume by destination, lead-time curves, cancellation rates) that let you sanity-check any model and explain the forecast to your director. Trade-off: No predictive number on its own; it is a prerequisite that makes the model trustworthy and cheaper to iterate. Effort: Low.

choices.title: Data preparation pipeline
choices.what: Transform the booking-level export into a clean destination–month panel with engineered features (rolling bookings, lead-time percentiles, cancellation flags, channel shares) ready for any forecasting method. You get: A reproducible recipe you can rerun each month; the panel becomes the single source of truth for the model, the analysis, and any future dashboard. Trade-off: Does not produce a forecast by itself; it is the foundation that makes the other two options reliable and fast to refresh. Effort: Low.

transcript.text: I am the head of marketing at a subscription company. The board asked for an AI segmentation of our customers, and I would like five or six segments with names we can put on a slide. The table I shared has one row per customer: signup date, the segment we already record, city, plan, tenure in months, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and whether they churned the next month. Next quarter my team can run at most three email campaigns: one to move people to a higher plan, one to keep people who look likely to leave, and one welcome series for new customers. The same person should not receive two of them. My campaign managers will use the segments to decide who gets which campaign. [shares customers.csv]

What I understood: you need 5–6 AI–discovered customer segments with presentation-ready names, so your campaign managers can assign each segment to exactly one of three email campaigns next quarter (upgrade, retention, welcome) with no customer receiving two.

Approach: the table has the right behavioral signals (tenure, spend, tickets, plan, city, signup date) to let unsupervised learning find natural groups that the existing “segment” column may not capture. I’d also audit the current segments first — if they already separate the three campaign audiences cleanly, you save time. Once segments exist (new or current), we design the mutually-exclusive assignment rules your email tool needs.

Plan (3–5 steps):
1. Quick audit of the existing segment column against the three campaign targets (upgrade potential, churn risk, new-customer share) — tells us whether it’s already usable.
2. If needed, run AI segmentation on the behavioral features to produce 5–6 named segments with profiles (size, avg spend, tenure, churn rate, top plan/city).
3. Validate that the segments cleanly separate the three campaign audiences; if overlap exists, note it.
4. Design the assignment rules: which segment → upgrade, which → retention, which → welcome, which → none, with a priority tie-breaker so no one gets two.
5. Deliver: segment label on every row, one-page segment profiles for the board slide, and the campaign assignment table for your managers.

Here are three ways to proceed — pick one, or tell me to combine them:

choices.title: AI Segmentation — 5–6 behavioral segments with slide-ready names
choices.what: Run unsupervised learning on all customer features (tenure, spend, tickets, plan, city, signup date) to discover 5–6 natural segments. DCLab profiles each segment with sizes, key metrics, and gives each a business-friendly name (e.g., “High-Value Loyalists”, “At-Risk High Spenders”, “New Explorers”). You get: A segment label on every customer row, a one-page segment profile table (size, avg spend, tenure, churn rate, top plan, top city), and 5–6 named segments ready for your board slide. Trade-off: Finds patterns the existing segment column may miss, but segments are data-driven — you’ll need to validate they map cleanly to your three campaigns. Effort: One project run; results in minutes.

You get: A report showing each current segment’s size, upgrade readiness, churn rate, and new-customer share — so you see instantly whether the current segments already separate the three campaign audiences. Trade-off: Fast and uses what you already have; but if the current segments blur the campaign audiences, you’ll still need new ones. Effort: One query; results in seconds.

You get: A decision table your campaign managers can implement in the email tool: segment → campaign (or none), with overlap counts and a priority rule. transcript.text: I am a data scientist at a company that sells accounting software to small firms. Two years ago we built a model that scores every new lead on how likely it is to become a customer, and the sales team calls the highest scores first. Since the autumn the sales team says the top leads are much worse than they used to be, and my manager wants me to retrain with a larger model and more features. Some context on the data: since the summer, part of our leads comes from a partner marketplace; we moved to a new CRM in August, and two form fields the model uses are no longer collected; and finance now counts a lead as converted when a free trial starts, where before it was the first payment. I have the old training set and every lead since, not yet exported. What would you do?

You've described a classic **label shift + covariate shift + feature loss** problem all at once. The manager's instinct (bigger model, more features) risks overfitting on shifted data without fixing the root causes.

**What's really happening**
1. **Label definition changed** (payment → trial start). Your old model learned "willing to pay"; the new target is "willing to try". These are different populations — trial starters include many who never pay.
2. **New lead source** (partner marketplace) since summer — different intent, different feature distributions.
3. **Two features gone** after CRM migration — the model now sees `NaN` where it once saw signal.
4. **Autumn degradation** lines up with all three changes compounding.

**What I'd do (in order)**

1. **Quantify the shifts before any retraining**
   - Compare feature distributions: pre-August vs post-August, marketplace vs direct, by month.
   - Compare conversion rates (old label *and* new label) by source and month.
   - Check calibration: does the old model's score still rank-order trial-starts? Does it rank-order payments?

2. **Decide on the target**
   - If you have enough post-August leads with *payment* outcomes, keep the old label (payment) — it's the business outcome that matters.
   - If not, retrain on trial-start but **calibrate** the scores to expected payment probability (use a second-stage model or isotonic regression on the subset that reaches payment).

3. **Handle the missing features**
   - Drop the two gone fields — retraining without them is cleaner than imputing.
   - Engineer replacements from what the new CRM *does* capture (e.g., enrichment data, behavioral signals from the trial).

4. **Retrain with time-aware validation**
   - Split by time (e.g., train on Jan–Jul, validate on Aug–Oct, test on Nov+).
   - Use a model class no more complex than the data supports (gradient boosting with early stopping, not a larger net).
   - Monitor **calibration curves** and **lift at top decile**, not just AUC.

5. **Shadow-test before handing to sales**
   - Run new scores alongside old for 2–4 weeks. Compare contact rates, trial rates, payment rates at each score band.
   - Only switch when the new model beats the old on *payment* lift in the top decile.

transcript.text: I am the operations lead at a tour company. Each month I tell our local partners how many guides to reserve in each destination for the month after next. If I reserve too few, we hire freelancers at the last minute for about three times the price; if I reserve too many, we pay a small fee for each guide we do not use. My director asked me for a machine learning model that forecasts how many bookings we will receive per destination each month. The table I shared is our booking export up to late February 2026: one row per booking with the booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether it had free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. I will use the result myself every month to fix the reservation. [shares bookings.csv]

**Problem**  
You decide every month how many guides to reserve for each destination for the month after next. The decision is made by you (operations lead) and the output is a single number per destination: the forecasted bookings for that future month. The moment of decision is the end of the current month (e.g., late March for May). You know all bookings made up to that date — their booking dates, travel dates, destinations, and a handful of attributes. You do not know how many additional bookings will arrive before the travel month starts. Under‑forecasting forces last‑minute freelancer hires at roughly three times the regular cost; over‑forecasting incurs a small fee per unused guide. The asymmetry means the forecast should be biased slightly high, but not wildly so.

**Approaches**  

| Approach | What it does | Cost to build / maintain | What you get |
|----------|--------------|--------------------------|--------------|
| **No model – fixed rule** (e.g., “same as last year” or “average of last 3 months”) | Zero engineering; you copy a historical number. | Negligible. | A baseline that ignores current booking pace, seasonality shifts, and channel changes. Likely large errors when demand deviates. |
| **Time‑series forecast per destination** (ARIMA, ETS, Prophet, or a tree‑based model on month‑level aggregates) | Uses the series of total monthly bookings per destination. | Moderate: need to aggregate, handle seasonality, retrain monthly. | Captures long‑term trend and seasonality but discards the bookings already on the books for the target month. |
| **Pickup / booking‑curve model** (recommended) | For each destination and travel month, models the final bookings as a function of cumulative bookings observed at specific lead times (e.g., 60, 30, 15 days before travel). Uses the booking_date and travel_date to reconstruct the booking curve for every past travel month. | Moderate‑high: requires reshaping the data into a panel of (destination, travel_month, lead_time) with cumulative counts, then training a model (e.g., gradient boosting or a simple regression) that predicts final bookings from partial curves. | Exploits the most relevant signal — how many bookings have already materialised for the target month — while still learning the typical shape of the booking curve from history. Naturally adapts to early/late booking patterns and can incorporate covariates (channel mix, nationality mix, price tier, free‑cancellation share) observed up to the decision date. |
| **Full demand model with external data** (adds search trends, marketing spend, events) | Predicts bookings from leading indicators before any bookings exist. | High: needs external data pipelines, feature engineering, ongoing maintenance. | Could forecast further ahead, but for your “month after next” horizon the booking curve already contains most of the information. Extra complexity unlikely to pay off. |

**Chosen approach: Pickup / booking‑curve model**  
It directly uses the information you have at decision time (bookings already made for the target month) and learns from historical curves how the remaining bookings usually materialise. It respects the cost asymmetry by allowing you to adjust the prediction interval (e.g., forecast the 75th percentile instead of the mean).

**Plan**  

1. **Define the decision cutoff**  
   - For each month you make the decision (call it *decision_month*), the target is *travel_month = decision_month + 2*.  
   - The cutoff date is the last day of *decision_month* (or the day you actually send the numbers). All bookings with *booking_date ≤ cutoff* and *travel_date in travel_month* are “on the books”.

2. **Build the training panel from history**  
   - From the raw bookings (up to Feb 2026), create a row for every (destination, travel_month) that has fully elapsed (i.e., travel_month ≤ Feb 2026).  
   - For each such row, compute the **final bookings** (count of non‑cancelled bookings with that travel_month).  
   - Choose a set of lead‑time anchors (e.g., 60, 45, 30, 15, 7 days before the first day of travel_month). For each anchor, compute the **cumulative bookings** made by that date (again non‑cancelled).  
   - Optionally add covariates measured at each anchor: share of bookings by channel, by nationality, average price, free‑cancellation rate, etc.  
   - The panel now has: destination, travel_month, final_bookings, cumulative_60, cumulative_45, …, covariates_at_60, covariates_at_45, …

3. **Train the pickup model**  
   - Target: final_bookings.  
   - Features: the cumulative bookings at the anchors (most recent anchor will be the one just before your decision cutoff), plus any covariates.  
   - Model: start with a simple linear model (final ~ cumulative_at_decision_anchor) per destination, then try a pooled gradient‑boosting model (e.g., LightGBM) with destination as a categorical feature.  
   - Because under‑forecasting is costlier, train with a quantile loss (e.g., 0.75 quantile) or add a small upward bias after the fact.

4. **Validate with a rolling‑origin scheme**  
   - Sort travel_months chronologically. For each month *t* (starting after a minimum history window), train on all months < *t*, predict for *t*, compare to actual final_bookings.  
   - Metrics: MAE, RMSE, and **asymmetric cost** = 3 × (under‑forecast) + 1 × (over‑forecast) where under/over are in guide units.  
   - Check that the model beats the “same as last year” and “average of last 3 months” baselines on the asymmetric cost.

5. **Produce the monthly forecast**  
   - At decision time (end of March for May), compute the cumulative bookings for May up to that date for each destination.  
   - Feed those cumulatives (and current covariates) into the trained model to get the forecasted final bookings.  
   - Round to whole guides and apply your bias (e.g., add 5 % or use the 75th percentile prediction).

6. **Monitor and retrain**  
   - Each month, after the travel month ends, add the new (destination, travel_month) row to the panel.  
   - Retrain the model quarterly or when the rolling‑origin MAE degrades by more than 10 % relative to the best observed.  
   - Stop retraining if the model hasn’t improved over the simple baseline for two consecutive quarters — then fall back to the baseline.

**What each step needs**  
- Step 1‑2: SQL/Python to reshape the 1500‑row booking export; no external data.  
- Step 3: A standard ML library (scikit‑learn, LightGBM); compute resources are tiny.  
- Step 4: A script that loops over past months; can run in minutes.  
- Step 5: A monthly notebook or scheduled job that reads the latest bookings, computes cumulatives, calls the model, outputs a CSV per destination.  
- Step 6: A log of monthly errors; a simple alert if asymmetric cost rises.

**When to stop**  
- If the pickup model’s asymmetric cost is not consistently better than the “last year same month” rule over a full seasonal cycle (12 months), revert to the rule and reconsider.  
- If the model works, keep it running with quarterly retraining; only revisit the approach if the business changes (e.g., new destinations, shift to online‑only channels) or the data volume grows substantially.

I am the head of marketing at a subscription company. The board asked for an AI segmentation of our customers, and I would like five or six segments with names we can put on a slide. The table I shared has one row per customer: signup date, the segment we already record, city, plan, tenure in months, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and whether they churned the next month. Next quarter my team can run at most three email campaigns: one to move people to a higher plan, one to keep people who look likely to leave, and one welcome series for new customers. The same person should not receive two of them. My campaign managers will use the segments to decide who gets which campaign. [shares customers.csv]

**Problem**  
You need a customer segmentation that serves two masters:  
* the board wants a tidy set of five or six named segments for a slide, and  
* your campaign managers must use those same segments to pick **exactly one** of three email campaigns (upsell, retention, welcome) for each customer next quarter, with no customer receiving two campaigns.  

The decision is **which campaign each customer gets**; the users are your three campaign managers; the unit is a customer; the moment is the start of next quarter. You know each customer’s tenure, plan, spend, recent support tickets, and whether they churned last month. You do **not** know how the board will judge the segments, nor the exact capacity or creative for each campaign.

**Approaches**  

| Approach | What it gives | Cost / effort |
|---|---|---|
| **Business-rule segmentation** – write explicit rules (tenure, plan, spend, tickets) that assign every customer to *at most one* campaign, then wrap those rules in memorable names. | Directly actionable, zero overlap, fully explainable to board and managers. | Low – a few hours with your analysts and campaign leads. |
| **Unsupervised clustering (k‑means, hierarchical)** – group customers on the numeric/categorical features, then map clusters to campaigns. | Data‑driven “AI” label; may reveal unexpected groups. | Medium – cleaning, encoding, tuning k, then manual mapping to campaigns; risk that clusters don’t align with your three campaigns. |
| **Supervised propensity models** – build three binary classifiers (churn risk, upsell propensity, new‑customer engagement) and assign each customer to the campaign with highest predicted lift. | Optimises each campaign’s target metric. | High – needs labelled history, model training, monitoring; still requires a tie‑break rule to avoid dual assignment. |
| **No model / status‑quo** – keep using the existing “segment” column. | Zero work. | Fails the board’s request and likely doesn’t match the three campaigns. |

**Chosen approach: Business-rule segmentation**  
It is the only method that guarantees the **mutual‑exclusion** constraint, is instantly usable by campaign managers, and can be dressed in the named segments the board expects.

**Plan**  

1. **Align on campaign priority** (1 hr workshop)  
   *Decide the pecking order when a customer qualifies for more than one campaign* (e.g., retention > upsell > welcome). Document the rule.

2. **Draft eligibility rules** (2 hrs with analysts)  
   Use the fields you have:  
   - **Welcome**: tenure ≤ 3 months (or first‑quarter flag from signup_date).  
   - **Retention**: high churn risk – e.g., support_tickets_90d ≥ 2 **or** monthly_spend dropped > 20% vs. prior quarter (if history exists) **or** churned_next_month=1 in recent data.  
   - **Upsell**: tenure > 3 months, on a lower‑tier plan, monthly_spend in top quartile of that plan, support_tickets_90d = 0.  
   - **No‑campaign**: everyone else.

3. **Assign every customer to one segment** (script in SQL/Python, 30 min)  
   Apply the priority order so each customer lands in **exactly one** of:  
   - *New Explorers* (welcome)  
   - *At‑Risk Champions* (retention)  
   - *Ready‑to‑Grow* (upsell)  
   - *Steady Core* (no campaign)  
   - *High‑Value Advocates* (top tier, high spend, low tickets – no campaign)  
   - *Quiet Newcomers* (new but low engagement – welcome variant)  
   (Adjust names/count to hit five or six.)

4. **Validate with campaign managers** (1 hr review)  
   - Check segment sizes vs. campaign capacity.  
   - Confirm no customer appears in two segments.  
   - Verify that each segment’s profile matches the campaign creative.

5. **Build the board slide** (30 min)  
   One row per segment: name, size, key metrics (avg tenure, plan mix, spend, tickets), assigned campaign (or “nurture”). Add a one‑sentence persona.

6. **Hand off to campaign tools** (ongoing)  
   Export a list of `customer_id → segment → campaign` for the email platform. Schedule a quarterly refresh (repeat steps 2‑4).

**Stopping criteria**  
- All 1 200 customers assigned to exactly one segment.  
- Campaign managers sign off that the lists are usable.  
- Board deck delivered with the five/six named segments.  

**What I assumed vs. what you told me**  
- You gave the column names and row count; I assumed the “existing segment” column is not binding for the new campaigns.  
- I assumed you have the ability to compute spend changes (if not, drop that rule).  
- I assumed the three campaigns are the only ones running next quarter.  
- I did **not** invent any numbers (segment sizes, thresholds, quartiles) – those will come from your data in step 2.

*Moment* – scoring happens at lead creation; the “quality” judgment is about what happens later (conversion).

*What is not known*

Retrain on recent data with the *old* target definition** – use only leads that have reached first payment, keep the original feature set (impute missing fields), same model size. | Moderate effort (data prep, training, validation), moderate risk (if first‑payment leads are too few or delayed). | A model that is consistent with the original business definition; isolates the effect of feature drift and source mix. |
| **3. Retrain on recent data with the *new* target definition** – use trial‑start as label, impute missing fields, possibly add new features from the new CRM. | Moderate‑high effort (label alignment, feature engineering), higher risk (target changed, so model optimizes a different outcome). | A model aligned with how finance now measures conversion; but you must be sure trial‑start is a reliable proxy for revenue. |
| **4. Retrain with a larger model and more features** (manager’s request) – add all available fields from the new CRM, partner‑source indicators, etc., use a more complex algorithm. | High effort (feature engineering, tuning, validation), highest risk (overfitting, opacity, harder to maintain). | Potential uplift *if* the new features carry signal and the target is stable; but you won’t know if the gain comes from better features or just from fixing the earlier issues. |
| **5. Simple rule‑based fallback** – e.g., call all partner‑marketplace leads last, or prioritize by a few high‑signal fields that are still collected. | Very low effort, low risk. | Immediate stop‑gap for sales while you diagnose; also a baseline to beat. |

---

**Chosen approach and plan**  
*Start with Approach 1 (diagnostic audit) before any retraining.* The simultaneous changes make it likely that the degradation is partly or wholly a data/label issue, not a model‑capacity issue. Retraining blindly could bake in the new target definition or the missing fields and make things worse.

**Step‑by‑step plan**

1. **Export and align the recent lead data**  
   - Pull every lead from the new CRM since the summer (including partner‑marketplace leads).  
   - Map each field to the old schema; for the two missing form fields, create “missing” indicators and impute with a neutral value (e.g., median of training set).  
   - Tag each lead with its source (original vs. partner) and the CRM version (pre‑/post‑August).  

2. **Recreate both target definitions**  
   - *Old target*: flag leads that eventually made a first payment (use payment records).  
   - *New target*: flag leads that started a free trial (use trial‑start records).  
   - Note leads that have neither yet (censored) – exclude them from evaluation for now.  

3. **Score the recent leads with the *existing* model**  
   - Apply the two‑year‑old model exactly as it was (same preprocessing, same feature list).  
   - Compute calibration curves, AUC, precision@top‑k, and conversion rates by score decile *separately* for:  
     a) original source vs. partner source  
     b) pre‑CRM vs. post‑CRM  
     c) old target vs. new target  

4. **Analyze the gaps**  
   - If performance drops mainly on partner leads → source shift.  
   - If performance drops on all leads but only under the new target → label shift (trial‑start ≠ payment).  
   - If performance drops only after August and only for the two missing fields → feature loss.  
   - If the model is well‑calibrated on the old target for original-source leads → the core model still works; the problem is external.  

5. **Decide next step based on evidence**  
   - *If source shift dominates*: build a separate model or add a source indicator; keep the old target.  
   - *If label shift dominates*: agree with finance on which target the business actually wants to optimize (trial‑start may not equal revenue).  
   - *If feature loss dominates*: either re‑engineer those fields (ask product to reinstate) or retrain without them.  
   - *If multiple factors*: prioritize fixing the biggest one first, then retrain a *similarly sized* model on recent data with the chosen target and available features.  

6. **Validation before deployment**  
   - Hold out the most recent month as a temporal test set.  
   - Compare the new candidate model (or the old model with fixes) against the simple rule‑based baseline (Approach 5).  
   - Require that the new model beats the baseline on *both* targets (or the agreed target) and shows stable calibration across sources.  

7. **Stopping rule**  
   - Stop the diagnostic when you can attribute >80 % of the performance gap to one or two concrete causes (source, label, features).  
   - Stop retraining when the candidate model’s improvement over the baseline is statistically significant and practically meaningful (e.g., lifts top‑decile conversion by a clear margin) *and* passes the cross‑source calibration check.

- *I assumed*: that “worse” means lower conversion among top‑scored leads; that you can access payment and trial‑start records to reconstruct both targets; that the two missing fields can be imputed or flagged; that the sales team would accept a short rule‑based fallback while you investigate; and that the manager’s request for a larger model is a hypothesis, not a requirement.

I am the credit risk manager at a consumer lender that finances phone and appliance purchases in shops. Today a rulebook written by our underwriters approves about 40 percent of applications. Management wants to grow, so they asked me for a machine learning model that predicts default for every applicant, to replace the rulebook and approve more people safely. We have about 60,000 past loans with the application form, the bureau score and whether the loan defaulted within 12 months, and I can export them next week. For the applications we rejected we kept the form and the bureau score, nothing more. The model would decide each new application automatically at the shop counter. How should I go about it?

**Problem**  
You need a decision system that, at the moment a shopper applies at the counter, estimates the probability that this applicant will default within 12 months. The system will replace the current rulebook (which approves roughly 40 % of applications) and is expected to approve more applicants while keeping default risk acceptable. The unit of decision is a single application; the moment is real‑time at the point of sale.  

What you know:  
- 60 000 past loans that were approved, each with the application form, the bureau score, and a 12‑month default flag.  
- For the applications that were rejected you have only the form and the bureau score — no outcome, because no loan was granted.  

What you do not know:  
- How the rejected applicants would have performed if they had been approved.  
- Whether the relationships between form variables, bureau score, and default are the same in the rejected population as in the approved population.  
- The exact approval‑rate target or the maximum tolerable default rate that management has in mind.  

---

**Approaches and what they cost / give**  

| Approach | What it does | Main cost / risk | What you get |
|----------|--------------|------------------|--------------|
| **1. Train only on approved loans** | Fit a default model on the 60 k approved records and apply it to everyone. | Strong selection bias: the model learns default risk *conditional on having passed the rulebook*. It will underestimate risk for applicants who look like the rejected group. | A model quickly, but unsafe for automatic approval of previously rejected profiles. |
| **2. Reject inference (augmentation / extrapolation)** | Assign provisional default labels to rejected applications using assumptions (e.g., “rejected applicants are X % riskier than similar approved ones”), then retrain on the combined set. | Requires untestable assumptions; results can be sensitive to the chosen method. | A model that covers the full applicant space, provided the assumptions are roughly right. |
| **3. Two‑stage modelling (propensity + outcome)** | First model the probability of being approved (propensity) using all applications; then model default only on approved loans, using the propensity as a covariate or weight. | Still relies on the assumption that, conditional on the observed variables, approval is independent of potential default. | A model that adjusts for selection on observables; transparent diagnostics. |
| **4. Champion‑challenger deployment with randomisation** | Keep the rulebook as champion. Deploy the new model as challenger on a small, randomly selected fraction of applications (e.g., 5 %). Over time, compare default rates and gradually increase the challenger’s share. | Requires operational setup and time to accumulate outcomes; you still need an initial model to deploy. | Real‑world evidence on model performance, safe growth, and a path to full replacement. |
| **5. Collect fresh labels via targeted approvals** | Approve a random sample of applicants who would have been rejected, solely to observe their outcomes. | Direct credit loss on the sample; needs governance approval and time (12 months for outcomes). | Unbiased data for the rejected region — the only way to fully remove selection bias. |

---

**Chosen approach**  
Start with **Approach 3 (two‑stage modelling with propensity weighting)** to build an initial model that corrects for selection on the variables you observe. Validate it rigorously on out‑of‑time and segmented hold‑outs. Then move to **Approach 4 (champion‑challenger with a small randomisation)** so you gather real outcomes on the model’s own decisions. In parallel, design **Approach 5 (targeted random approvals)** for the next planning cycle to obtain clean labels for the rejected region. This sequence balances speed, safety, and long‑term bias reduction.

---

**Plan — steps in order, what each needs, how to check, when to stop**

1. **Data export & inventory** (week 1)  
   - Pull the 60 k approved loans and all rejected applications from the same period.  
   - Verify column definitions, missingness, and that the 12‑month default flag is defined identically for all approved loans.  
   - *Check*: row counts match expectation; no duplicate application IDs; bureau score and form fields are present for both sets.  
   - *Stop if*: data quality issues cannot be resolved in a few days.

2. **Define the modelling target & splits** (week 1)  
   - Target = binary default within 12 months of origination.  
   - Create time‑based splits: e.g., oldest 70 % for training, next 15 % for validation, most recent 15 % for out‑of‑time test. Keep the same splits for approved and rejected sets.  
   - *Check*: default rates are stable across splits; no look‑ahead leakage.  
   - *Stop if*: strong time trends suggest non‑stationarity that a static model cannot handle.

3. **Build the propensity model** (week 2)  
   - Use *all* applications (approved + rejected) to predict “approved by rulebook” from form + bureau score.  
   - Algorithm: gradient‑boosted trees or logistic regression with regularisation — choose the simpler one that yields good calibration.  
   - *Check*: AUC on validation; calibration plot (predicted vs. observed approval rate) in deciles.  
   - *Stop if*: propensity model cannot separate approved from rejected (AUC ≈ 0.5) — then selection on observables is weak and weighting adds little.

4. **Build the default model on approved loans with propensity weighting** (week 2‑3)  
   - Train a default predictor on approved loans only, using form + bureau score as features.  
   - Weight each approved loan by the inverse of its estimated approval propensity (stabilised weights).  
   - Algorithm: same family as propensity model; tune hyper‑parameters on weighted validation loss.  
   - *Check*:  
     - Weighted validation AUC and Brier score.  
     - Calibration on the validation set (reliability diagram).  
     - Compare predictions for approved vs. rejected applicants in the validation period — the model should not output systematically lower risk for rejected profiles unless justified by features.  
   - *Stop if*: calibration is poor on the rejected‑like segment (e.g., predicted default < 1 % for a group where external benchmarks suggest > 5 %).

5. **Define decision rule & policy simulation** (week 3)  
   - Choose a probability cutoff that approximates the current 40 % approval rate on the validation set.  
   - Simulate: apply cutoff to validation set; compute approval rate, predicted default rate among approved, and expected portfolio default rate.  
   - *Check*: the simulated portfolio default rate is at or below the current rulebook’s realised default rate (which you can compute from the 60 k loans).  
   - *Stop if*: no cutoff yields a higher approval rate without increasing predicted portfolio default.

6. **Champion‑challenger pilot design** (week 3‑4)  
   - Agree with operations on a randomisation fraction (e.g., 5 % of incoming applications routed to the model, rest to rulebook).  
   - Build monitoring dashboard: daily approval rate, 30‑day/90‑day/12‑month default tracking (as far as maturity allows), population stability index on input features.  
   - *Check*: pilot can be implemented in the decision engine without latency > 200 ms.  
   - *Stop if*: engineering constraints prevent real‑time scoring.

7. **Launch pilot & monitor** (week 5 onward)  
   - Run pilot for at least 3 months (or until ~2 000 model‑scored applications have matured to 90 days).  
   - Monthly review: compare observed early‑default rates between model and rulebook cohorts, adjusting for any covariance shift.  
   - *Decision gate*: if model cohort’s 90‑day default rate is not statistically higher than rulebook’s, and approval rate is higher, prepare plan to increase model share. If worse, revert and diagnose.

8. **Plan targeted random approvals for next cycle** (parallel, months 1‑3)  
   - Work with credit committee to approve a small random sample (e.g., 1‑2 % of rejected‑like applicants) regardless of score.  
   - Track their 12‑month outcomes.  
   - *Check*: sample size and governance sign‑off.  
   - *Stop if*: risk appetite or regulatory constraints block it.

9. **Model retraining with enriched data** (after 12 months)  
   - Incorporate the pilot outcomes and the targeted‑approval outcomes into a single training set that now has labels for a representative slice of the full applicant population.  
   - Retrain without propensity weighting (or with lighter weighting).  
   - Validate again on a fresh out‑of‑time window.  
   - *Check*: improved calibration on previously rejected profiles; stable or better AUC.  
   - *Stop if*: no measurable improvement — then the current model is sufficient for now.

---

**Key boundaries**  
- All numbers above (split ratios, pilot fraction, sample sizes) are illustrative — you will set them with your team.  
- The plan assumes the bureau score and form variables capture the main risk drivers; if you later add new data sources, revisit step 3.  
- No assumption is made about management’s exact approval‑rate or default‑rate targets; the simulation in step 5 makes the trade‑off explicit so they can decide.
